q.stem: Which of these is NOT part of the UK?
q.exp: The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The Republic of Ireland is a separate, independent country.

q.stem: Why was Mary, Queen of Scots, executed in 1587?
q.exp: Elizabeth I kept Mary in prison for nearly 20 years. Mary was executed because people believed she was plotting to take the English throne.

opts.t: She was suspected of plotting against Queen Elizabeth I
She refused to pay taxes to the English government
She led a French army to attack London
She surrendered Scotland to the Spanish king

q.stem: What is the term for the belief that kings are chosen by God and do not have to answer to Parliament?
q.exp: King James I and his son Charles I believed in the "Divine Right of Kings". This meant they thought only God could judge their actions, which angered Parliament.

q.stem: In which year was the National Health Service (NHS) set up?
q.exp: The NHS began in 1948 under the Labour government. Aneurin (Nye) Bevan, the Minister for Health, led its creation.
On Valentine's Day, 14 February, people send cards or gifts to someone they love.

q.stem: Dame Kelly Holmes won two gold medals at the 2004 Olympic Games in Athens in which sport?
q.exp: Dame Kelly Holmes won Olympic gold in both the 800 metres and 1,500 metres middle-distance running events.

q.stem: What are the senior members of the main opposition party called when they mirror the roles of government ministers?
q.exp: Members of the Shadow Cabinet look at the work of government ministers. They propose different ideas and policies for their party.
After a general election, the Monarch asks the leader of the party with the most members in the House of Commons to form a government.

q.stem: What was the name of the area in eastern and northern England where Viking laws applied?
q.exp: The region ruled by Viking laws was known as the Danelaw. King Alfred defeated the Vikings and agreed to split England with them.

q.stem: Where did Saint Patrick go as a missionary to spread Christianity, later becoming its patron saint?
q.exp: Saint Patrick was born in Britain but went to Ireland as a missionary. He is now celebrated as the patron saint of Ireland.

q.stem: Which prize is given each year to a contemporary British artist?
q.exp: The Turner Prize is named after the painter J M W Turner and celebrates contemporary art. The Man Booker Prize is for fiction.

q.stem: Which 20th-century British composer wrote 'The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra'?
q.exp: Benjamin Britten is one of the most famous British classical composers of the 20th century. He also founded the Aldeburgh Festival.

q.stem: What is one way people can help support their local school in the UK?
q.exp: Parents and other people in the community can volunteer as school governors. They help to manage the school's budget and plan its future.

opts.t: By setting the local education tax

CH2-UK.body:
The **United Kingdom** is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. **Great Britain** means England, Scotland and Wales only.

The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are **Crown dependencies**. They have a special link to the UK but their own governments.

The UK Parliament is in London. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland also have their own parliament or assembly with **devolved** powers.
facts: UK = England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
Great Britain = England, Scotland and Wales
Crown dependencies: Channel Islands, Isle of Man

CH3-C20.body:
The **First World War** (1914–1918) ended at 11 am on 11 November 1918. The Battle of the Somme in 1916 caused huge losses.

In the **Second World War** (1939–1945) Winston Churchill became Prime Minister in 1940. Soldiers were rescued from **Dunkirk**, the RAF won the **Battle of Britain**, and Allied forces landed in Normandy on **D-Day**, 6 June 1944.

After 1945 Clement Attlee's government created the welfare state and the **NHS** in 1948. British inventions of the time include penicillin, the jet engine and radar.
facts: 11 November 1918: end of the First World War
1940: Dunkirk and the Battle of Britain
Fleming: penicillin; Whittle: jet engine; Turing: computing

CH3-EAR.body:
The first people in Britain were hunter-gatherers. Farmers came later and built monuments such as **Stonehenge** in Wiltshire. **Skara Brae** on Orkney is a well-preserved Stone Age village.

The Romans invaded in **AD 43** and stayed until **AD 410**. Boudicca, queen of the Iceni, fought against them. Hadrian's Wall kept out the Picts.

Next came the Anglo-Saxons, then the Vikings from Denmark and Norway. Alfred the Great defeated the Vikings. In **1066** William of Normandy won the Battle of Hastings.
facts: AD 43: Roman invasion under Emperor Claudius
Sutton Hoo, Suffolk: Anglo-Saxon royal ship burial
1066: Battle of Hastings; recorded in the Bayeux Tapestry
Domesday Book: William's survey of England

CH3-TUD.body:
**Henry VIII** broke away from the Church of Rome and set up the Church of England. He had six wives. His daughter **Elizabeth I** defeated the **Spanish Armada** in 1588. William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564.

In 1603 James VI of Scotland also became James I of England. **Charles I** fought Parliament in the **Civil War** (Cavaliers against Roundheads) and was executed in 1649. Oliver Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector.

The monarchy returned in 1660. The Great Fire of London was in 1666. In 1688 the **Glorious Revolution** brought William of Orange to the throne, and in **1707** the Act of Union created Great Britain.
facts: 1707: Act of Union creates Great Britain

CH4-ART.body:
The UK has a rich culture. The **Proms** are classical concerts held mainly at the Royal Albert Hall. Famous composers include Purcell, Elgar and Britten.

Famous writers include Shakespeare, Jane Austen, Charles Dickens and Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. The **Turner Prize** is for contemporary art and the **Man Booker Prize** is for fiction.

Sir Christopher Wren designed St Paul's Cathedral. Wales holds the **Eisteddfod**, a festival of music, poetry and performance.
facts: Dickens: Oliver Twist; Austen: Pride and Prejudice

CH4-CUS.body:
Important Christian festivals are **Christmas** (25 December) and **Easter**. Boxing Day is 26 December. Other faiths' festivals, such as Diwali, Eid al-Fitr, Hanukkah and Vaisakhi, are celebrated too.

Other traditions include New Year (Hogmanay in Scotland), Valentine's Day (14 February), April Fool's Day (1 April, jokes until midday), Halloween (31 October) and Bonfire Night (5 November).

On **Remembrance Day**, 11 November, people wear poppies to remember those who died in wars.
facts: Hogmanay: New Year's Eve in Scotland
Bonfire Night, 5 November: the 1605 Gunpowder Plot

CH4-SPO.body:
Sport is important in UK life. Football, rugby and cricket are popular, and England and Australia play cricket for **The Ashes**.

**Wimbledon** is the oldest tennis tournament in the world. **St Andrews** is the home of golf. The **Grand National** horse race is at Aintree, near Liverpool.

London hosted the Olympics in 1908, 1948 and 2012. The Paralympics grew from work at **Stoke Mandeville** hospital. Famous sportspeople include Sir Roger Bannister and Sir Steve Redgrave.

CH5-CON.body:
The UK constitution is not written in a single document. The UK is a **constitutional monarchy**: the monarch is head of state, but the elected government makes decisions.

**Parliament** has two Houses. The **House of Commons** has elected MPs. The **House of Lords** is not elected and includes life peers, some hereditary peers and senior bishops.

A general election is held at least every **five years**. The **Speaker** chairs debates in the Commons and stays neutral.
facts: Constitution: not written in one document
General election at least every five years

CH5-ROL.body:
You can take part in your community in many ways: voting, volunteering, serving on a jury and helping your neighbours.

To vote you must be on the **electoral register**. People on the register may be called for **jury service**.

Working people pay income tax and **National Insurance**, which helps pay for the State Pension and the NHS. You must be at least **17** to drive a car.
facts: Electoral register: the list of voters
National Insurance helps pay for the State Pension and the NHS
Minimum age to drive a car: 17
